title: How Many Kinds of Principalities There Are, and by What Means They Are Acquired
coreMove: Sort the possession by form, origin, prior habits, and military basis before choosing any rule for it.
sourcePressure: The source is a compact decision tree. It separates all states into republics and principalities, then divides principalities into hereditary, new, and annexed possessions, asks whether subjects were used to freedom or princely rule, and asks whether acquisition came by one's own arms, others' arms, fortune, or ability.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The wrong version treats the opening as a generic preface about power. The writer must make it a diagnostic sorting act where every later prescription depends on the labels attached at the start.

hook: a broad opening about ruthless leaders or timeless power
a modern executive staring at an org chart and learning to be strategic
a chapter-by-chapter preview of the whole book
counterintuition: most people assume power is about personality, but actually it is classification
all leadership situations are basically the same until you choose tactics
tryThisNow: set a timer for ninety seconds and list your power bases
write down a goal and decide whether to be bold
think of a leader you admire and copy their style

exampleSpecs.domain: a provisional governor receiving three towns after a border treaty
exampleSpecs.audience: a civilian administrator who wants to announce one uniform policy on the first morning
exampleSpecs.stakes: one town has elected councils, one obeyed a duke, and one was attached to the old crown by marriage, so a single decree could create three different rebellions
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before signing the tax notice, the governor pins three seals on the wall, moves the free town under republic, the ducal town under principality, and the marriage town under annexed member, then crosses out the single policy order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Three wax seals lie on a treaty map beside an unsigned tax notice.

exampleSpecs.domain: a naval prize court deciding what authority captured harbor islands had lived under
exampleSpecs.audience: a judge advocate sorting reports before recommending occupation rules
exampleSpecs.stakes: mislabeling elected harbor councils as former royal dependencies would send troops to solve a problem that needs preserved local law
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The advocate places a harbor charter, a royal appointment, and a captain's surrender note into separate trays labeled free, princely, and won by another's arms before drafting any order.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A salt-stained harbor charter curls at the edge of a court table.

exampleSpecs.domain: a museum repatriation board classifying the governing claims behind disputed city bronzes
exampleSpecs.audience: curators deciding whom to negotiate with after a regime change
exampleSpecs.stakes: returning the bronzes to the loudest ministry could ignore a city that had governed the shrine under its own civic law
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The board stops debating ownership rhetoric and circles the old civic statutes, the royal inventory stamp, and the militia seizure date in different colors to classify the claim before naming a counterparty.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A bronze horse tag rests on a photocopy of old civic statutes.

exampleSpecs.domain: an election observer mission entering a province after a coup and a negotiated restoration
exampleSpecs.audience: field observers who must decide which local actors can certify turnout
exampleSpecs.stakes: the province may be a restored hereditary administration, a newly seized capital, or a free district coerced by soldiers, and each label changes the risk report
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The team leader asks observers to predict the category, then turns over three evidence cards: family governor retained, council dissolved, garrison installed by outside troops.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Laminated polling-station cards sit under a cracked plastic evidence box.

exampleSpecs.domain: a monastic land steward reviewing estates after an abbot inherits and purchases neighboring valleys
exampleSpecs.audience: a steward tempted to use the same rent roll for old abbey lands and newly acquired villages
exampleSpecs.stakes: ancestral tenants, purchased lands, and villages used to their own councils will react differently to the same levy
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before copying last year's levy, the steward lays the abbey rent roll beside the purchase deed and the village council bell, then marks inherited, new, and accustomed to freedom in the margin.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A brass council bell sits on top of a folded purchase deed.

exampleSpecs.domain: a peacekeeping logistics cell mapping who actually won control of checkpoints after a ceasefire
exampleSpecs.audience: officers deciding whether authority rests on local forces, allied troops, or accidental collapse
exampleSpecs.stakes: a checkpoint held by local fighters can be negotiated differently from one held because a foreign brigade handed over the gate
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The colonel stops the briefing at the phrase under control and makes the analyst put colored pins for own arms, others' arms, fortune, and ability on each checkpoint before approving supplies.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Colored map pins are scattered beside a ceasefire checkpoint grid.

skillTargets: classify a possession as republic or principality before choosing a governing response
distinguish hereditary, entirely new, and annexed principalities in short political scenarios
infer why prior freedom, prior obedience, own arms, others' arms, fortune, and ability change the next move
evaluate whether a proposed policy skipped the opening taxonomy and therefore overreaches

tryThisNowSpec: Take one institution in the news and label it in four columns: form of rule, old or new possession, prior habit of the people, and basis of control. Stop before recommending any action.
